questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{p\sin 2x + 1 - \cos 2x}{x + \tan x}\right) = 1$ then the value of '$p$' is
questions.solution:
The given limit is $\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{p\sin 2x + 1 - \cos 2x}{x + \tan x}\right) = 1$.

Substituting $x = 0$, we get the form $\dfrac{0}{0}$.

Applying L'Hospital's rule by differentiating the numerator and the denominator with respect to $x$:

$\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{2p\cos 2x + 2\sin 2x}{1 + \sec^2 x}\right) = 1$

Substituting $x = 0$ into the expression:

$\dfrac{2p\cos(0) + 2\sin(0)}{1 + \sec^2(0)} = 1$

$\dfrac{2p(1) + 0}{1 + 1} = 1$

$\dfrac{2p}{2} = 1$

$p = 1$

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is of the form $\dfrac{0}{0}$ as $x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $1 + \sin x$:

$\lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}} \left( \dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x} \times \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{1 + \sin x} \right)$

$= \lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}} \left( \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos x (1 + \sin x)} \right)$

$= \lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}} \left( \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x (1 + \sin x)} \right)$

$= \lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}} \left( \dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x} \right)$

Substituting $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$= \dfrac{0}{1 + 1} = 0$

Answer: $0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $\lim\limits_{x \to 3}\left[\dfrac{1}{x-3} + \dfrac{9x}{27-x^3}\right]$

Using the identity $a^3 - b^3 = (a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2)$, we can write $27 - x^3 = -(x^3 - 27) = -(x-3)(x^2+3x+9)$

Substituting this into the limit expression:

$\lim\limits_{x \to 3}\left[\dfrac{1}{x-3} - \dfrac{9x}{(x-3)(x^2+3x+9)}\right]$

Taking the common denominator:

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 3}\left[\dfrac{x^2+3x+9-9x}{(x-3)(x^2+3x+9)}\right]$

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 3}\left[\dfrac{x^2-6x+9}{(x-3)(x^2+3x+9)}\right]$

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 3}\left[\dfrac{(x-3)^2}{(x-3)(x^2+3x+9)}\right]$

Since $x \to 3$, $x \neq 3$, we can cancel the common factor $(x-3)$ from the numerator and the denominator:

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 3}\left[\dfrac{x-3}{x^2+3x+9}\right]$

Substituting $x = 3$ into the simplified expression:

$= \dfrac{3-3}{3^2+3(3)+9}$

$= \dfrac{0}{27} = 0$

Answer: $0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\dfrac{(1 - \cos 2x)(3 + \cos x)}{x\tan 4x}$

Using the trigonometric identity $1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x$:

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\dfrac{2\sin^2 x(3 + \cos x)}{x\tan 4x}$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $x^2$:

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\dfrac{2\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2(3 + \cos x)}{\dfrac{\tan 4x}{x}}$

$= \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\dfrac{2\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2(3 + \cos x)}{4\left(\dfrac{\tan 4x}{4x}\right)}$

Using the standard limits $\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ and $\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\tan \theta}{\theta} = 1$:

$= \dfrac{2(1)^2(3 + \cos 0)}{4(1)}$

$= \dfrac{2(4)}{4} = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given the limit $L = \lim _{x \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{\sec ^2 x-2}{\tan x-1}$.

Using the identity $\sec ^2 x = 1 + \tan ^2 x$, the expression becomes:

$L = \lim _{x \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{1 + \tan ^2 x - 2}{\tan x - 1}$

$L = \lim _{x \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{\tan ^2 x - 1}{\tan x - 1}$

Factoring the numerator as a difference of squares:

$L = \lim _{x \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{(\tan x - 1)(\tan x + 1)}{\tan x - 1}$

Canceling the common term $(\tan x - 1)$ for $x \neq \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$L = \lim _{x \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{4}} (\tan x + 1)$

Substituting $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$L = \tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2$.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $L = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sqrt{1-\cos 2 x}}{x \sqrt{2}}$.

Using the trigonometric identity $1 - \cos 2x = 2 \sin^2 x$, we have $\sqrt{1 - \cos 2x} = \sqrt{2 \sin^2 x} = \sqrt{2} |\sin x|$.

Substituting this into the expression, $L = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sqrt{2} |\sin x|}{x \sqrt{2}} = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{|\sin x|}{x}$.

Evaluating the left-hand limit as $x \rightarrow 0^{-}$: $L^{-} = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \dfrac{-\sin x}{x} = -1$.

Evaluating the right-hand limit as $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$: $L^{+} = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.

Since the left-hand limit is not equal to the right-hand limit, the limit does not exist.

Answer: does not exist

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta$. As $\theta \rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x \rightarrow 0$.

Substituting $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$, we have $\sin \theta = \sin(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x) = \cos x$ and $\cos \theta = \cos(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x) = \sin x$.

The limit becomes $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{x \sin x}$.

Using the identity $1 - \cos x = 2 \sin^2(\dfrac{x}{2})$, the expression is $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{2 \sin^2(\dfrac{x}{2})}{x \sin x}$.

Dividing numerator and denominator by $x^2$, we get $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{2 \left(\dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x}\right)^2}{\dfrac{\sin x}{x}} = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2}{\dfrac{\sin x}{x}}$.

Since $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, the limit is $\dfrac{2 \cdot (1/2)^2}{1} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \dfrac{x^4-1}{x-1}=\lim _{x \rightarrow k} \dfrac{x^3-k^3}{x^2-k^2}$, then the value of K is
questions.solution:
Evaluate the first limit:
$\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \dfrac{x^4-1}{x-1} = \lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \dfrac{(x-1)(x^3+x^2+x+1)}{x-1} = \lim _{x \rightarrow 1} (x^3+x^2+x+1) = 1+1+1+1 = 4$.

Evaluate the second limit:
$\lim _{x \rightarrow k} \dfrac{x^3-k^3}{x^2-k^2} = \lim _{x \rightarrow k} \dfrac{(x-k)(x^2+xk+k^2)}{(x-k)(x+k)} = \lim _{x \rightarrow k} \dfrac{x^2+xk+k^2}{x+k} = \dfrac{k^2+k^2+k^2}{k+k} = \dfrac{3k^2}{2k} = \dfrac{3k}{2}$.

Equate the two limits:
$4 = \dfrac{3k}{2}$.

Solve for $k$:
$3k = 8 \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{8}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{8}{3}$

Differentiating using product rule:

$f'(x) = 2x \sin x + x^2 \cos x$

At $x = a$:

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $f(x) = (1-x)^n$. The given limit is of the form $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{f(x) - f(0)}{x - 0}$, which is the definition of the derivative $f'(0)$.

Calculate the derivative of $f(x) = (1-x)^n$ with respect to $x$:

$f'(x) = n(1-x)^{n-1} \times \dfrac{d}{dx}(1-x) = n(1-x)^{n-1} \times (-1) = -n(1-x)^{n-1}$

Evaluate the derivative at $x = 0$:

$f'(0) = -n(1-0)^{n-1} = -n(1)^{n-1} = -n$.

Answer: $-n$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 3 x+e^{2 x}-1}{x}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 3 x+e^{2 x}-1}{x}$
Put $x=0 \Rightarrow \frac{\sin 0+e^0-1}{0}\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)$
Using L'hospital's rule we can differentiate both Numerator and denominator separately
$\therefore \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{3 \cos 3 x+2 e^{2 x}}{1}$
Now put $x=0$
$=\frac{3 \cos 0+2 e^0}{1}=3+2=5$

questions.solution:
Put $x=0$
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \left(\frac{2+0}{2-0}\right)^{\frac{1}{0}}=1^{\infty} \\ \\ \therefore \quad & e^{\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{2+x}{2-x}-1\right) \times \frac{1}{x}} \\ \\ &[ \left.\therefore \lim _{x \rightarrow 0}[f(x)]^{g(x)}=e^{\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} g(x)[f(x)-1]}\right] \\ \\ & =e^{\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left[\frac{2+x-2+x}{x(2-x)}\right]} e^{\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{2}{2-x}} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $L = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin(a+x) - \sin(a-x)}{x}$.

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin C - \sin D = 2 \cos \left( \dfrac{C+D}{2} \right) \sin \left( \dfrac{C-D}{2} \right)$, we set $C = a+x$ and $D = a-x$.

Then $\dfrac{C+D}{2} = \dfrac{a+x+a-x}{2} = a$ and $\dfrac{C-D}{2} = \dfrac{a+x-(a-x)}{2} = x$.

Substituting these into the expression, we get $L = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{2 \cos a \sin x}{x}$.

Since $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, the expression simplifies to $2 \cos a \times 1 = 2 \cos a$.

Answer: $2 \cos a$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a^x - b^x}{c^x - d^x}$.

Since the limit is of the form $\dfrac{0}{0}$ as $x \rightarrow 0$, we apply L'Hopital's rule by differentiating the numerator and the denominator with respect to $x$.

The derivative of $a^x$ is $a^x \ln a$.

Applying the rule:

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dx}(a^x - b^x)}{\dfrac{d}{dx}(c^x - d^x)} = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a^x \ln a - b^x \ln b}{c^x \ln c - d^x \ln d}$.

Evaluating the limit as $x \rightarrow 0$:

$L = \dfrac{a^0 \ln a - b^0 \ln b}{c^0 \ln c - d^0 \ln d} = \dfrac{\ln a - \ln b}{\ln c - \ln d}$.

Using the property of logarithms $\ln x - \ln y = \ln(\dfrac{x}{y})$:

$L = \dfrac{\ln(\dfrac{a}{b})}{\ln(\dfrac{c}{d})}$.

This is equivalent to $\dfrac{\log(\dfrac{a}{b})}{\log(\dfrac{c}{d})}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\log \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)}{\log \left(\dfrac{c}{d}\right)}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the distinct roots of $a x^2+b x+c=0$, then $\lim _\limits{x \rightarrow \alpha} \dfrac{1-\cos \left(a x^2+b x+c\right)}{(x-\alpha)^2}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Thus, $ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)$.

The limit is given by $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow \alpha} \dfrac{1 - \cos(a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta))}{(x - \alpha)^2}$.

Using the identity $1 - \cos \theta = 2 \sin^2(\theta/2)$, we have $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow \alpha} \dfrac{2 \sin^2(\dfrac{a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)}{2})}{(x - \alpha)^2}$.

Using the standard limit $\lim_{u \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin u}{u} = 1$, we multiply and divide by the square of the argument of the sine function:

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow \alpha} 2 \left[ \dfrac{\sin(\dfrac{a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)}{2})}{\dfrac{a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)}{2}} \right]^2 \times \dfrac{a^2(x - \alpha)^2(x - \beta)^2}{4(x - \alpha)^2}$.

As $x \rightarrow \alpha$, the term in the square brackets approaches 1. The expression simplifies to:

$L = 2 \times 1^2 \times \dfrac{a^2(x - \beta)^2}{4} = \dfrac{a^2(\alpha - \beta)^2}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{a^2(\alpha-\beta)^2}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The limit is of the form $\dfrac{0}{0}$ as $x \rightarrow 1$.

Using L'Hopital's rule, we differentiate the numerator and the denominator with respect to $x$:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 1} \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{15} - 1)}{\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{10} - 1)} = \lim_{x \rightarrow 1} \dfrac{15x^{14}}{10x^9}$

Simplifying the expression:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 1} \dfrac{15}{10} x^{14-9} = \dfrac{3}{2} \lim_{x \rightarrow 1} x^5$

Substituting $x = 1$:

$\dfrac{3}{2} \times (1)^5 = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \left( \dfrac{\sin ax}{\sin bx} \right)^k$.

We can rewrite the expression inside the limit as:

$\dfrac{\sin ax}{\sin bx} = \dfrac{\sin ax}{ax} \cdot \dfrac{bx}{\sin bx} \cdot \dfrac{ax}{bx}$

Using the standard limit $\lim_{\theta \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1$, we have:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin ax}{ax} = 1$ and $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{bx}{\sin bx} = 1$.

Therefore, $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin ax}{\sin bx} = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \left( \dfrac{\sin ax}{ax} \cdot \dfrac{bx}{\sin bx} \cdot \dfrac{a}{b} \right) = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{a}{b}$.

Applying the power $k$ to the limit:

$L = \left( \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sin ax}{\sin bx} \right)^k = \left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right)^k$.

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^k$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let the given limit be $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\sqrt{a+x} - \sqrt{a}}{x \sqrt{a(a+x)}}$.

Rationalizing the numerator by multiplying and dividing by $(\sqrt{a+x} + \sqrt{a})$:

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{(\sqrt{a+x} - \sqrt{a})(\sqrt{a+x} + \sqrt{a})}{x \sqrt{a(a+x)}(\sqrt{a+x} + \sqrt{a})}$

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{(a+x) - a}{x \sqrt{a(a+x)}(\sqrt{a+x} + \sqrt{a})}$

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{x}{x \sqrt{a(a+x)}(\sqrt{a+x} + \sqrt{a})}$

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a(a+x)}(\sqrt{a+x} + \sqrt{a})}$

Substituting $x = 0$ into the expression:

$L = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a(a+0)}(\sqrt{a+0} + \sqrt{a})}$

$L = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2}(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{a})}$

$L = \dfrac{1}{a(2\sqrt{a})}$

$L = \dfrac{1}{2 a \cdot a^{\dfrac{1}{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{2 a^{\dfrac{3}{2}}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2 a^{\dfrac{3}{2}}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{e^{a x}-e^{b x}}{2 x}$ is equal to
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{e^{a x}-e^{b x}}{2 x} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\left(1+a x+\frac{(a x)^2}{2 !}+\frac{(a x)^3}{3 !}+\ldots\right)}{-\left(1+b x+\frac{(b x)^2}{2 !}+\frac{(b x)^3}{3 !}\right)} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\left[\begin{array}{c}\left.(a-b)+\left(\frac{a^2 x}{2 x}+\frac{a^3 x^2}{3 !}+\ldots\right)\right] \\ \left.+\left(\frac{b^2 x}{2 !}+\frac{b^3 x^2}{3 !}+\ldots\right)\right] \\ 2 x\end{array}\right]}{\left[\begin{array}{c}3 ! \\ 2 x\end{array}\right]}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2}[(a-b)+(0+0+\ldots)+(0+0+\ldots)] \\ & =\frac{a-b}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{x^2-2 x+1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)^{2 x}$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { Let } L=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{x^2-2 x+1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)^{2 x} \\ & \Rightarrow \ln L=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left[2 x \ln \left(\frac{x^2-2 x+1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \ln L=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left[2 x \ln \left(1+\frac{2 x-1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \ln L=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left[2 x\left(\frac{2 x-1}{x^2-4 x+2}-\frac{\left(\frac{2 x-1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)^2}{2}+\right.\right. \\ & \left.+\frac{\left(\frac{2 x-1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)^3}{3}\right) \ldots .\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad \ln L=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2 x(2 x-1)}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)-0+0 . \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \ln L=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{4 x^2\left(1-\frac{1}{2 x}\right)}{x^2\left(1-\frac{4}{x}+\frac{2}{x}\right)} \\ & \quad \ln L=\frac{4(1-0)}{(1-0+0)} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \ln L=4 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad L=e^4\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a^x - b^x}{x}$.

Rewrite the expression by adding and subtracting $1$ in the numerator:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{(a^x - 1) - (b^x - 1)}{x}$

Using the property of limits, this can be split into two separate limits:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a^x - 1}{x} - \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{b^x - 1}{x}$

Recall the standard limit formula $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{k^x - 1}{x} = \ln k$.

Applying this formula to both terms:

$\ln a - \ln b$

Using the logarithmic property $\ln a - \ln b = \ln \left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right)$, the result is $\log \left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right)$.

Answer: $\log \dfrac{a}{b}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\lim _\limits{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{e^{a x}-e^{b x}}{2 x}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The limit is given by $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{e^{ax} - e^{bx}}{2x}$.

Since the limit is of the form $\dfrac{0}{0}$ as $x \rightarrow 0$, L'Hopital's rule can be applied by differentiating the numerator and the denominator with respect to $x$.

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{ax} - e^{bx})}{\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x)}$

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{ae^{ax} - be^{bx}}{2}$

Substituting $x = 0$ into the expression:

$L = \dfrac{ae^{0} - be^{0}}{2} = \dfrac{a - b}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{a-b}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\lim _\limits{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\dfrac{x^2-2 x+1}{x^2-4 x+2}\right)^{2 x}$ is
questions.solution:
The limit is of the form $1^{\infty}$ as $x \rightarrow \infty$.

Let $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \left(\dfrac{x^2-2x+1}{x^2-4x+2}\right)^{2x}$.

Using the formula $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} [f(x)]^{g(x)} = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow a} g(x)[f(x)-1]}$, we have:

$L = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} 2x \left(\dfrac{x^2-2x+1}{x^2-4x+2} - 1\right)}$

$L = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} 2x \left(\dfrac{x^2-2x+1 - (x^2-4x+2)}{x^2-4x+2}\right)}$

$L = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} 2x \left(\dfrac{2x-1}{x^2-4x+2}\right)}$

$L = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{4x^2-2x}{x^2-4x+2}}$

Dividing numerator and denominator by $x^2$:

$L = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{4 - 2/x}{1 - 4/x + 2/x^2}} = e^{4/1} = e^4$.

Answer: $e^4$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{\left(1+a^3\right)+8 e^{1 / x}}{1+\left(1-b^3\right) e^{1 / x}}=2$, then
questions.solution:
Let $L = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{(1+a^3)+8 e^{1 / x}}{1+(1-b^3) e^{1 / x}}$.

Consider the limit as $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$. As $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$, $1/x \rightarrow \infty$, so $e^{1/x} \rightarrow \infty$.

Dividing the numerator and denominator by $e^{1/x}$, we get:

$L = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \dfrac{(1+a^3)e^{-1/x} + 8}{e^{-1/x} + (1-b^3)} = \dfrac{0 + 8}{0 + (1-b^3)} = \dfrac{8}{1-b^3}$.

Given $L = 2$, we have $\dfrac{8}{1-b^3} = 2$, which implies $1-b^3 = 4$, so $b^3 = -3$, or $b = -3^{1/3}$.

Now consider the limit as $x \rightarrow 0^{-}$. As $x \rightarrow 0^{-}$, $1/x \rightarrow -\infty$, so $e^{1/x} \rightarrow 0$.

$L = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \dfrac{(1+a^3)+8 e^{1 / x}}{1+(1-b^3) e^{1 / x}} = \dfrac{(1+a^3) + 0}{1 + 0} = 1+a^3$.

Given $L = 2$, we have $1+a^3 = 2$, which implies $a^3 = 1$, so $a = 1$.

Thus, $a=1$ and $b=-3^{1/3}$.

Answer: $a=1, b=-3^{1 / 3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is of the form $1^{\infty}$. We use the formula $\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} (f(x))^{g(x)} = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} g(x)(f(x)-1)}$.

Here, $f(x) = 1 + \dfrac{a}{x} + \dfrac{b}{x^2}$ and $g(x) = 2x$.

The limit becomes $e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} 2x \left(1 + \dfrac{a}{x} + \dfrac{b}{x^2} - 1\right)} = e^{\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} 2x \left(\dfrac{a}{x} + \dfrac{b}{x^2}\right)}$.

Simplifying the expression inside the exponent:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} 2x \left(\dfrac{ax + b}{x^2}\right) = \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{2ax^2 + 2bx}{x^2} = \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \left(2a + \dfrac{2b}{x}\right) = 2a$.

We are given that the limit is $e^2$, so $e^{2a} = e^2$.

Equating the exponents, $2a = 2$, which gives $a = 1$.

The value of $b$ does not affect the limit as $\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{2b}{x} = 0$ for any finite $b$.

Therefore, $a = 1$ and $b$ can be any real number.

Answer: $a=1, b \in R$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given limit is $L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a - \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{4}}{x^4}$.

Using the binomial expansion for $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} = a \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}} = a \left( 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2a^2} - \dfrac{x^4}{8a^4} - \dfrac{x^6}{16a^6} - \dots \right)$ for small $x$.

Substituting this into the expression:

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a - a \left( 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2a^2} - \dfrac{x^4}{8a^4} - \dots \right) - \dfrac{x^2}{4}}{x^4}$

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a - a + \dfrac{x^2}{2a} + \dfrac{x^4}{8a^3} + \dots - \dfrac{x^2}{4}}{x^4}$

$L = \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{x^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{2a} - \dfrac{1}{4} \right) + \dfrac{x^4}{8a^3} + O(x^6)}{x^4}$

For the limit $L$ to be finite, the coefficient of $x^2$ must be zero, so $\dfrac{1}{2a} - \dfrac{1}{4} = 0$.

Solving for $a$, we get $\dfrac{1}{2a} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, which implies $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$.

Answer: $a=2$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{a^{x}+b^{x}+c^{x}}{3}\right)^{2 / x},(a, b, c\gt 0)$ is
questions.solution:
As $x \to 0$, the base $\dfrac{a^x+b^x+c^x}{3} \to 1$ and exponent $\dfrac{2}{x} \to \infty$, giving $1^\infty$ indeterminate form.

Using $\lim f(x)^{g(x)} = e^{\lim g(x)[f(x)-1]}$:

$L = e^{\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{2}{x}\left(\dfrac{a^x+b^x+c^x}{3}-1\right)} = e^{\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{a^x+b^x+c^x-3}{x}\right)}$

$= e^{\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{a^x-1}{x}+\dfrac{b^x-1}{x}+\dfrac{c^x-1}{x}\right)}$

Using $\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{k^x - 1}{x} = \ln k$:

$L = e^{\dfrac{2}{3}(\ln a + \ln b + \ln c)} = e^{\dfrac{2}{3}\ln(abc)} = e^{\ln(abc)^{2/3}} = (abc)^{2/3}$

This does not match options (1), (2), or (3). The answer is (4) None of these.

We have,

\begin{aligned}
&\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} x \sin \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sin \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)}{\left(\frac{2}{x}\right)} \times 2 \\
&\text { Put } \frac{2}{x}=y . \\
&\text { Then } x \rightarrow \infty \\
&\Rightarrow \frac{2}{x} \rightarrow 0 \Rightarrow y \rightarrow 0 \\
&\therefore \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sin \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)}{\left(\frac{2}{x}\right)} \times 2 \\
&\quad=\lim _{y \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin y}{y} \times 2=1 \times 2=2
\end{aligned}

questions.q: If $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{e^{x}-1}{4 x} & \text { for } x \neq 0 \\ \frac{k+x}{4} & \text { for } x=0\end{array}\right.$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $k=$
questions.solution:
$\because f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$
\begin{aligned}
&\text { So, } \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)=f(0) \\
&\Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{e^{3 x-1}}{4 x}=\frac{k+0}{4} \\
&\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{4} \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} 3\left(\frac{e^{3 x}-1}{3 x}\right)=\frac{\bar{k}}{4} \\
&\Rightarrow \quad 3 \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{e^{3 x}-1}{3 x}=k \Rightarrow 3 \times 1=k \Rightarrow k=3
\end{aligned}
